study.title: Ranks and the process group
study.locator: Minutes 5:15 to 5:20: what torchrun assigns as global and local rank and why a process group is created

focus: Global rank \(r\) with \(0 \le r < W\) names one process in a run of \(W\) processes. Local rank names the same process inside its node. World size \(W\) is the process count, not the GPU count.
`RANK`, `WORLD_SIZE` and `LOCAL_RANK` come from the launcher. `MASTER_ADDR` and `MASTER_PORT` tell every process where rank 0 waits for the handshake.
Plan one process per GPU and set the device from the local rank, as in `torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank)`. Two ranks sharing one GPU serialize kernels and break the one-device-per-rank NCCL setup.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, map 2 nodes with 4 GPUs each under one launcher job of 8 processes: the world size, the global ranks on each node, each rank's local rank, and the device each rank sets. Then state which rank holds local rank value 1 on the second node.
traps: Reading local rank as global rank on the second node. Local ranks restart at 0 on each node.
Launching more processes than GPUs and assigning two ranks to one device. NCCL expects one device per rank.
Setting WORLD_SIZE to a value that disagrees with the spawned process count. The init handshake waits for processes that never arrive.

selfTest.q: Two nodes hold 4 GPUs each and one job launches 8 processes. Which global ranks sit on node 1, and what is the local rank of global rank 6?
selfTest.a: Node 1 holds global ranks 4 to 7. Rank 6 has local rank 2 and uses the third GPU of that node.

selfTest.q: What does `dist.init_process_group` exchange between processes?
selfTest.a: Only handshake locations through the master address and port, a shared file, or a TCP endpoint. No tensors move; setup only makes later communication possible.

selfTest.q: A snippet calls `dist.all_reduce(tensor, dst=0)`. Why is that wrong?
selfTest.a: `dist.all_reduce` takes no `dst` argument, and every rank keeps the reduced result. The `dst` argument belongs to `dist.reduce`, whose result is valid only on the root.

selfTest.q: Two ranks share one GPU and both call NCCL collectives. What breaks?
selfTest.a: The one-device-per-rank setup breaks. Kernels from both ranks serialize on the shared device, and the communicator is built per device, so sharing is unsupported even when it appears to start.

study.title: Steps 1 to 3 with diffs and the Part 1 video
study.locator: step2_process_group_manager and step3_dataloader with their diffs and the Part 1 video on the model, the process group manager and the dataloader
study.depth: Rebuild the rank grid yourself before reading the solution.

focus: A store is a key-value handshake, either `TCPStore` or `FileStore`. The launcher starts the processes, rendezvous introduces them, and `dist.init_process_group` builds the world group.
The default group holds all \(W\) ranks. `dist.new_group` carves named subsets, one rank may belong to several groups at once, and each group orders its own collectives.
Picotron lays ranks out as `torch.arange(world).view(dp, pp, cp, tp)` and enumerates one subgroup per axis. Every rank must build the identical grid or the groups disagree silently.
File init needs a nonexistent or empty shared file with fcntl locking. Mesh shapes must match on all ranks or setup hangs.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, take world size 4 with dp 2 and tp 2 in Picotron axis order: write the tensor-parallel groups and the data-parallel groups as rank sets.
traps: Reusing one fixed MASTER_PORT for several concurrent runs. The second job fails or joins the wrong rendezvous, so use a distinct port per run.
Trusting a LOCAL_RANK fallback of the form `global_rank % world_size` in example code on multiple nodes. It is not the true node-local rank.
Assuming subgroups inherit a barrier or an ordering from the world group. Each group needs its own calls in the same order.

selfTest.q: What does the store do, and when is it no longer needed?
selfTest.a: It exchanges handshake locations so ranks can find each other during init. After the process group is built, collectives use direct links and no longer consult the store.

selfTest.q: World size 4 with dp 2 and tp 2 in Picotron order: which ranks share a tensor-parallel group, and which share a data-parallel group?
selfTest.a: Tensor-parallel groups are {0, 1} and {2, 3}. Data-parallel groups are {0, 2} and {1, 3}.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 of a subgroup calls `all_reduce` but rank 1 of the same subgroup calls `broadcast`. What happens?
selfTest.a: Both hang. Every member of a group must issue the same collective sequence, and subgroups do not inherit ordering from the world group.

selfTest.q: Two jobs on one machine share MASTER_PORT. What goes wrong?
selfTest.a: The second job either fails to bind or rendezvous with the wrong peers. Give each run its own port.

study.title: Send, receive and pipeline handoffs
study.locator: Minutes 7:08 to 7:10: send and receive as point-to-point primitives, with the pipeline send at minutes 9:59 to 10:00 as the use case

focus: Every `dist.send` names a dst and every `dist.recv` names a src, with a preallocated buffer of matching shape and dtype on the receiving rank. Blocking calls return after completion; immediates return a `Work` handle that requires `req.wait()`.
After `dist.isend`, writing the sent tensor is undefined until wait. After `dist.irecv`, reading the receive buffer is undefined until wait. After wait, the transfer is guaranteed.
Broadcast copies one source tensor to all ranks. Reduce combines every rank into dst only, so other ranks hold stale data after the call.
A send with no matching receive, or a receive with no send, blocks forever. The matched pair is the unit that must agree.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the two-process exchange: rank 0 builds a 3-element tensor and sends it to rank 1 with isend and irecv plus wait, then rank 1 broadcasts it back so both ranks hold it. State every buffer each rank allocates.
traps: Allocating the receive buffer with the wrong shape or dtype. The call may hang or corrupt instead of raising.
Reading a reduce result on a non-root rank. Only dst holds the combined value.
Reusing a send buffer right after isend without wait. The transfer may still be in flight.

selfTest.q: What is the observable difference between `dist.send` with `dist.recv` and `dist.isend` with `dist.irecv`?
selfTest.a: The blocking pair returns after the transfer completes. The immediate pair returns a `Work` handle at once, and the transfer is only guaranteed after `req.wait()`.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 calls isend on a tensor, then overwrites the tensor before wait. Rank 1 receives after its own wait. What can rank 1 hold?
selfTest.a: Anything, including a mix of old and new values. Writing a sent buffer before wait is undefined behaviour.

selfTest.q: Four ranks call `dist.reduce` with `dst=0` and `SUM`. Afterwards rank 2 reads its tensor. What does it see?
selfTest.a: Its own stale input. Only rank 0 holds the combined sum after a reduce.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 sends to rank 1, but rank 1 never posts a receive and instead calls `all_reduce`. What happens?
selfTest.a: Both hang. The send waits for a matching receive that never comes, and rank 1 waits at a collective rank 0 never joins.

study.title: Ring costs for all-gather, reduce-scatter and all-reduce
study.locator: Section 8.1, Communication Primitives (pp. 40 to 41): the ring all-gather, ring reduce-scatter and ring all-reduce costs in the rendered equations

focus: Ring all-reduce is a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather. With \(N\) ranks and payload \(S\), each half moves \(\frac{N-1}{N} S\) bytes per rank, so all-reduce moves \(2 \frac{N-1}{N} S\).
Gradient averaging is `dist.all_reduce(param.grad.data, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)` on every rank, then division by the world size. The sum is collective; the division is local.
All-gather takes one tensor per rank and returns a length-\(N\) list on every rank. Reduce-scatter takes a list of per-rank inputs and returns one shard per rank.
The tutorial ring challenge sends full buffers, not chunks. Chunking into \(N\) pieces is what turns its \((N-1) S\) cost into the ring cost above.
units.reproduce: By hand, take 4 ranks and a 1 GB payload: reduce-scatter moves 0.75 GB per rank, all-gather moves 0.75 GB per rank, and ring all-reduce moves 1.5 GB per rank. Then run all three on 4 gloo CPU processes and match every rank against the single-process sums.
traps: Passing one stacked tensor to `dist.reduce_scatter`. It takes a list of per-rank input tensors and raises a type error otherwise.
Forgetting the division by world size after a SUM all-reduce. Every update then silently uses a learning rate scaled by worker count.
Treating reduce-scatter as a cheaper drop-in for all-reduce. It returns only one shard per rank; the all-gather half is still owed.

selfTest.q: Four ranks all-reduce a 1 GB gradient buffer. How many payload bytes cross each rank, and how does that compare with a naive full-buffer ring?
selfTest.a: Ring all-reduce moves \(2 \times 3/4 \times 1\) GB = 1.5 GB per rank. A naive ring that forwards full buffers moves \((4-1) \times 1\) GB = 3 GB per rank, twice as much.

selfTest.q: Why does the tutorial divide by size after the all-reduce instead of before it?
selfTest.a: The collective must sum identical-scale local gradients first so every rank holds the same total. Division is then a local rescale on each rank; dividing before would still work arithmetically but the shared pattern is sum collectively, rescale locally.

selfTest.q: Two ranks hold [1, 2, 3, 4] and [10, 20, 30, 40]. What does each rank hold after reduce-scatter with SUM?
selfTest.a: Rank 0 holds [11, 22] and rank 1 holds [33, 44]: chunk 0 and chunk 1 of the elementwise sum.

selfTest.q: All-gather and reduce-scatter each move about half the bytes of all-reduce. When does that factor of 2 fail?
selfTest.a: For small latency-bound messages, where startup cost dominates bytes moved. The factor of 2 holds in the bandwidth-bound regime with equal payloads.

study.title: All-to-all meaning and the two-step exchange
study.locator: Minutes 9:57 to 10:00 for the all-to-all meaning, then minutes 19:22 to 19:24 for why one exchange carries counts and a second carries data
study.depth: Watch the semantics segments only. Skip the expert-parallel implementation around them; it belongs to the MoE section.

focus: All-to-all takes a list of per-destination inputs on each rank. Rank \(r\) receives chunk \(r\) from every source, concatenated in source-rank order, so each rank ends with a different mix.
All-reduce gives every rank the same aggregate. All-to-all gives each rank a different slice. Token routing needs the second pattern.
All-to-all fan-out grows as \(O(N^2)\) logical pairs, so contention bounds it where per-node bytes bound all-reduce. Small routed messages are latency-bound.
The gloo backend runs `dist.all_to_all` on CPU in PyTorch 2.14, although the backends table marks it unsupported. Test it instead of routing around it.
units.reproduce: By hand, take rank inputs `[[1, 2, 3, 4], [5, 6, 7, 8]]`: rank 0 receives `[1, 2, 5, 6]` and rank 1 receives `[3, 4, 7, 8]`. Then run `dist.all_to_all` on 2 gloo CPU processes and match both ranks.
traps: Assuming all-to-all concatenates like all-gather. All-gather gives every rank the same concatenation; all-to-all gives each rank its own chunk from each source.
Passing single tensors instead of per-rank lists. Both the input and the output of `dist.all_to_all` are lists with one entry per rank.
Planning uneven token splits without padding. Equal-size chunks are the CPU contract; ragged routing needs explicit padding or a dedicated layout later.

selfTest.q: Two ranks hold [1, 2, 3, 4] and [5, 6, 7, 8]. What does each rank hold after all-to-all?
selfTest.a: Rank 0 holds [1, 2, 5, 6] and rank 1 holds [3, 4, 7, 8]: chunk 0 from each source lands on rank 0, chunk 1 on rank 1.

selfTest.q: Why does expert routing use all-to-all rather than all-reduce?
selfTest.a: Each token must reach one specific expert rank, so destinations need distinct payloads. All-reduce would give every rank the same sum, which cannot route.

selfTest.q: Why is all-to-all contention-sensitive while ring all-reduce keeps constant per-node bytes?
selfTest.a: All-to-all opens a logical pair per rank pair, so pairs grow quadratically while all-reduce only talks to ring neighbours with constant bytes per node.

selfTest.q: The backends table marks gloo all-to-all unsupported. What should you do on CPU in PyTorch 2.14?
selfTest.a: Run it anyway. A 4-process gloo run of `dist.all_to_all` passes on 2.14.1, so the table entry is stale for CPU.

study.title: Barrier as a rendezvous point
study.locator: Minutes 13:17 to 13:19: all devices wait until every rank arrives at the barrier

focus: Every rank in a group must invoke the same collectives in the same order with agreeing shapes and dtypes. Any deviation hangs or corrupts, because there is no central scheduler to reconcile the calls.
`dist.barrier` blocks until all ranks in the group arrive. It synchronizes arrival only; it moves no tensors and fixes no data skew.

Conditional collectives, where only some ranks enter the call, are the classic hang. So are swapped orders, such as rank 0 calling all-reduce then broadcast while rank 1 calls broadcast then all-reduce.
`dist.monitored_barrier` with a short timeout plus `TORCH_DISTRIBUTED_DEBUG=DETAIL` names the rank that never arrived. The default 30-minute gloo timeout turns every hang into a long silence.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the order-swap drill on 2 gloo CPU processes with a 20-second timeout: rank 0 calls all-reduce then broadcast while rank 1 calls broadcast then all-reduce. Predict the timeout, then fix the order and show both calls pass.
traps: Using a barrier as if it synchronizes data. Ranks can arrive together and still hold different tensors.
Running hang drills with the default timeout. Set a timeout of seconds for drills; the 30-minute default is for production patience, not debugging.
Blaming the network for a shape mismatch hang. Agree shapes and dtypes first, then suspect links.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 calls all-reduce then broadcast; rank 1 calls broadcast then all-reduce with matching shapes. What happens?
selfTest.a: Both hang. Rank 0 waits for a broadcast partner while rank 1 waits for an all-reduce partner, and neither call can complete.

selfTest.q: All ranks call `dist.barrier` and proceed. Does that prove their tensors agree?
selfTest.a: No. The barrier only proves every rank arrived. Tensor agreement needs the right collectives with matching data, not arrival.

selfTest.q: A job hangs at a collective with the default gloo timeout. How long until it fails, and what finds the guilty rank faster?
selfTest.a: About 30 minutes. A short explicit timeout plus `monitored_barrier` and `DETAIL` debug output names the rank that never arrived within seconds.

selfTest.q: Only ranks with nonzero loss call all-reduce. Why is that unsafe even when the math looks conditional-safe?
selfTest.a: Collectives are group operations, not local branches. Ranks that skip the call leave the others waiting, so the condition must be reduced to all ranks first or every rank must enter the call.

study.title: Communication-computation overlap
study.locator: Communication-Computation Overlap with Layer-by-layer overlap, Bucket fusion and Overlap limits
study.depth: Read for the overlap vocabulary and the exposed-versus-hidden distinction. Leave bucket tuning for the data-parallelism section.

focus: Passing `async_op=True` returns a `Work` handle at once. The collective completes only after `handle.wait()`, and buffers on both sides are unsafe until then.
A CUDA stream orders work; an event marks a point in a stream. Dependencies between compute and communication streams, not mere async issue, decide what actually overlaps.
Overlap hides transfer time behind compute only when compute outlasts the transfer and no dependency forces a wait. Async issue without such cover is just deferred waiting.
CPU `time.perf_counter` around async calls measures issue overhead, not GPU concurrency. Event-attributed timelines on a GPU are the proof; treat CPU numbers as issue-cost examples only.
units.reproduce: On 2 gloo CPU processes, issue `dist.all_reduce` with `async_op=True`, run a fixed local matrix multiply, then wait and assert the reduced value. Time the same script with a blocking call and report both numbers as issue costs, not as overlap evidence.
traps: Reading the result tensor right after an async call without wait. The values are undefined until completion.
Claiming overlap from a shorter async wall time on CPU. The CPU returns early by construction; concurrency needs stream dependency proof on a GPU.
Forgetting device sync before reusing a buffer that an async NCCL collective still reads. With two or more GPUs, synchronize the stream, not just the Python thread.

selfTest.q: What does `dist.all_reduce` with `async_op=True` return, and when may the input buffer be reused?
selfTest.a: A `Work` handle. The buffer may be touched only after `handle.wait()` confirms completion.

selfTest.q: What is the difference between a CUDA stream and a CUDA event in overlap work?
selfTest.a: A stream orders queued work; an event records that a stream reached a point. Code waits on events to express that communication may proceed only after some compute finished.

selfTest.q: An async all-reduce script runs faster on CPU than its blocking twin. Does that prove communication overlapped with compute?
selfTest.a: No. The async call returns before the transfer finishes, so a shorter Python wall time only shows deferred waiting. Proof needs GPU timelines showing transfer and compute on overlapping intervals with satisfied dependencies.

selfTest.q: Where must the wait go if a second collective consumes the first collective's output?
selfTest.a: Between them on every rank that consumes the data. Issuing the consumer early reads an incomplete buffer.

units.title: Ring and tree collectives and the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) cost model
outcomes: Derive ring and tree all-reduce costs from the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) model and locate the crossover.
Classify a message as latency-bound or bandwidth-bound from its size against the crossover size.
Adjust a textbook prediction with the measured NCCL small-message overhead.
units.why: Algorithm choice is a size question, not a brand question. The same ring that wins on gigabyte gradients loses on kilobyte tokens, and the crossover is one equation.

next.note: Turn the byte counts into measured bandwidth with the bus correction.
Use the cost model inside a full parallel-plan budget.

study.locator: Mapping the Terrain with The \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) cost model, The LogP model and Theory vs. practice: The NCCL reality gap, then Engineering the Flow with Ring AllReduce, Tree AllReduce and The algorithm crossover point

study.title: Ring costs as rendered equations
study.locator: Section 8.1, Communication Primitives (pp. 40 to 41): the ring all-gather, reduce-scatter and all-reduce costs plus the alternate ring problem
study.depth: Read the rendered PDF, not an extracted text copy: the text layer drops fraction bars, so N-1 over N reads as N-1N.

study.title: Intra-node collective costs on GPUs
study.locator: How Do Collectives Work on GPUs, Intra-node collectives: the ring all-gather and reduce-scatter time approaching bytes over egress bandwidth

study.title: Unchunked ring sketch (page read 2026-10-14)
study.locator: Our Own Ring-Allreduce: the `isend` and `recv` ring with the `torch.chunk` exercise left to the reader

focus: Every message costs \(T(n) = \alpha + n / \beta\): a startup tax \(\alpha\) plus a transit fee per byte. The crossover size \(n^* = \alpha \beta\) separates latency-bound small messages from bandwidth-bound large ones.

Ring all-reduce costs \(2 (N-1) \alpha + 2 \frac{N-1}{N} \frac{S}{\beta}\): many latency steps but minimal bytes. Tree forms pay about \(\log N\) steps with more bytes per step, so trees win small and rings win large.
A naive ring that forwards full buffers costs \((N-1) S / W\), about \(N/2\) times the chunked ring. Chunking is the whole saving.
Measured NCCL small-message latency runs 7 to 8 times the wire \(\alpha\), so the real crossover sits above the textbook one. Measure effective \(\alpha\) on the target fabric before choosing.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive ring all-reduce time from reduce-scatter plus all-gather, then evaluate 4 ranks and a 1 GB payload at \(\alpha = 2\,\mu\text{s}\) and \(\beta = 50\) GB/s: latency 12 microseconds plus 30 ms of bandwidth, about 30.01 ms. Then state which side of the 100 KB crossover a 4 KB token message sits on.
traps: Quoting bandwidth only. Below the crossover size the byte count barely matters and startup dominates.
Treating reduce-scatter as twice as fast as all-reduce in general. The half-bytes factor holds only bandwidth-bound with equal payloads.
Copying TPU link constants from the scaling-book answers into NCCL predictions. Redo every answer with your own \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

selfTest.q: On a link with \(\alpha = 2\,\mu\text{s}\) and \(\beta = 50\) GB/s, what is the crossover size, and is a 4 KB MoE token message latency-bound or bandwidth-bound?
selfTest.a: The crossover is \(2 \times 10^{-6} \times 5 \times 10^{10} = 100{,}000\) bytes, about 100 KB. A 4 KB message sits 25 times below it, so it is latency-bound and fusing helps more than adding bandwidth.

selfTest.q: Derive the ring all-reduce bandwidth term from its two halves.
selfTest.a: Reduce-scatter moves \(\frac{N-1}{N} S\) bytes per rank and all-gather moves the same again, so the ring total is \(2 \frac{N-1}{N} \frac{S}{\beta}\) plus \(2 (N-1)\) latency steps.

selfTest.q: Four ranks reduce 1 GB with a naive full-buffer ring versus a chunked ring at 50 GB/s. What are the two times?
selfTest.a: Naive: \(3 \times 1\) GB / 50 GB/s = 60 ms. Chunked: \(2 \times 3/4 \times 1\) GB / 50 GB/s = 30 ms. The naive ring costs twice as much at 4 ranks.

selfTest.q: A textbook crossover says rings win above 1 MB, but NCCL measurements prefer trees up to several MB. Why?
selfTest.a: The textbook \(\alpha\) is the wire value. NCCL protocol setup inflates effective small-message latency several-fold, which pushes the real crossover upward.

units.title: Per-rank bytes, critical paths, message size and effective bandwidth
outcomes: Derive per-rank wire bytes and the critical path for all five core collectives.
Convert a measured time into algorithm bandwidth and bus bandwidth with the right correction factor.
Run a message-size sweep on CPU and separate the latency-flat sizes from the bandwidth-linear ones.
units.why: Vendor plots quote bus bandwidth while timers measure time. The correction factor between them decides whether a link is saturated or the algorithm is wasteful.

next.note: Use the same factors to diagnose exposed communication in step time.
Carry the byte counts into throughput and utilization arithmetic.

study.title: Algorithm bandwidth versus bus bandwidth
study.locator: Bandwidth with Algorithm bandwidth as S over t, Bus bandwidth with the per-collective correction table, and the AllReduce derivation

study.title: Benchmarking formulas and warmup discipline
study.locator: Benchmarking with `all_reduce` and `reduce_scatter`: the sent-bytes lines with the factor of 2 for all-reduce only, plus Section 5.1.1 of the assignment handout for 5 warmups and `torch.cuda.synchronize`

study.title: NCCL reality gap across message sizes
study.locator: Mapping the Terrain with Theory vs. practice: The NCCL reality gap, including the small-message overhead ratios and the large-message agreement

focus: Per-rank wire bytes with \(n\) ranks and payload \(S\): all-reduce \(2 \frac{n-1}{n} S\), all-gather and reduce-scatter \(\frac{n-1}{n} S\) each, broadcast and reduce \(S\) through the root bottleneck, all-to-all \(\frac{n-1}{n} S\) under contention.

Algorithm bandwidth is \(\text{algbw} = S / t\). Bus bandwidth multiplies by the correction factor: \(2 \frac{n-1}{n}\) for all-reduce, \(\frac{n-1}{n}\) for all-gather, reduce-scatter and all-to-all, and 1 for broadcast and reduce.
Small sizes show flat time against the latency floor; large sizes show time linear in bytes. The knee between them sits near the crossover size of the fabric.
CPU gloo sweeps show the shape of that knee and validate the byte factors. They say nothing about GPU link speeds, so never compare a gloo GB/s number with an NVLink or InfiniBand figure.
units.reproduce: On 4 gloo CPU processes, sweep all-reduce payloads from 4 KB to 16 MB with 5 warmups: plot time and bus bandwidth with the 1.5 correction factor, mark the flat and the linear regimes, and state the assumed crossover for comparison.
traps: Calling the TensorTonic `algorithm_bytes` a bus bandwidth. That problem counts ring wire bytes, while nccl-tests reserves algorithm bandwidth for S over t and applies the correction after.
Timing one shot without warmup or synchronization. First iterations pay setup cost and async calls return early, so both inflate bandwidth.
Comparing effective bandwidth across different rank counts without the correction. The factor removes the rank-count trend so the remainder reflects the hardware.

selfTest.q: Four ranks all-reduce 1024 bytes in 0.001 s. What are the modeled bytes per rank and the bandwidth?
selfTest.a: Bytes per rank are \(2 \times 1024 \times 3/4 = 1536\). Bandwidth is \(1536 / 0.001 = 1{,}536{,}000\) bytes/s.

selfTest.q: Why does the lecture benchmark double the sent bytes for all-reduce but not for reduce-scatter?
selfTest.a: Ring all-reduce performs both halves, reduce-scatter plus all-gather, while reduce-scatter performs only the reduction half. The factor of 2 counts the second pass.

selfTest.q: A sweep shows flat time up to 64 KB and linear time above 4 MB. Which regime is which, and what does the flat part measure?
selfTest.a: Flat is latency-bound and linear is bandwidth-bound. The flat part measures startup and software overhead, not link speed.

selfTest.q: Your 4-process gloo sweep reports 2 GB/s bus bandwidth. The book quotes 50 GB/s InfiniBand. Is your link 25 times slower?
selfTest.a: No comparison follows. The gloo number ran over loopback or TCP on CPU with different software overhead, so it cannot speak about the GPU fabric.

Read a node topology and NCCL debug output at the level of links, not just rank counts.

study.title: NCCL topology, algorithms and communicator lifecycle
study.locator: Chapter 4 Distributed Networking Communication: NCCL for Distributed Multi-GPU Communication, Topology Awareness in NCCL, NCCL Communication Algorithms, and NCCL Communicator Lifecycle and Environment Gotchas

focus: Inside a node, GPUs meet over NVLink and NVSwitch with PCIe to the host. Between nodes, NICs carry traffic over InfiniBand or Ethernet at an order less bandwidth. Keep the heavy bytes on the fast tier.
Use NCCL for CUDA tensors and Gloo for CPU tensors. NCCL needs one GPU per rank; Gloo runs the same collective vocabulary on CPU without GPU-tuned speed.
NVLink numbers come in pairs: about 900 GB/s bidirectional is 450 GB/s one-way, and only the one-way rate enters \(T(n) = \alpha + n / \beta\). Mixing the two doubles or halves every prediction.

Companion code `format_bandwidth` reports total gathered bytes over time for all-gather, which equals algorithm bandwidth, not bus bandwidth: https://github.com/cfregly/ai-performance-engineering/blob/b57e4c6a9e261c09ac09208705d040c81b03d35e/code/ch04/nccl_benchmark.py - multiply its all-gather rate by \((n-1)/n\) before comparing with bus-bandwidth figures.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, choose the backend for three runs: 4 CPU processes, 2 GPUs on one node, and 8 GPUs across 2 nodes. Name the tier each all-reduce mostly crosses and which bandwidth row of the book table governs it.
traps: Reading CPU gloo timings as interconnect evidence. They cross loopback or office TCP with CPU overhead, so they cannot speak about NVLink or InfiniBand.
Assuming one GPU is enough for multi-rank NCCL practice. One GPU means at most one NCCL rank; further ranks need more GPUs or the gloo CPU path.
Treating MPI as a pip-install backend. PyTorch binaries exclude it, so MPI needs a source rebuild and stays vocabulary here.

selfTest.q: Eight ranks span 2 nodes of 4 GPUs. Which tier should carry the bulk of an all-reduce, and why?
selfTest.a: The intra-node NVLink tier. A hierarchical plan reduces inside each node first and sends only shards between nodes, because the inter-node tier is far slower per byte.

selfTest.q: Four CPU processes need broadcast and all-reduce. Which backend, and what changes with 4 GPUs?
selfTest.a: Gloo on CPU. With 4 GPUs use NCCL with one GPU per rank, since NCCL carries the GPU-tuned collectives and Gloo GPU paths are unoptimized.

selfTest.q: A table quotes 900 GB/s for NVLink. What value enters the \(\alpha\)-\(\beta\) formula, and why?
selfTest.a: 450 GB/s one-way. The formula counts bytes in one direction, while 900 GB/s is the bidirectional total.

selfTest.q: `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` shows `NET/IB` for some ranks and `NET/Socket` for others. What does that tell you?
selfTest.a: Traffic split across tiers: some ranks use InfiniBand and some fall back to sockets. Placement or interface settings disagree across the run.

study.locator: How to diagnose NCCL multi-gpu and multi-node connectivity issues with `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO`, How to check if P2P is supported, How to count NCCL calls, and Useful NCCL Debug Environment Variables

study.title: Process-group timeout and teardown
study.locator: Minutes 5:37 to 5:38: setting a higher timeout at group creation, lowering it later, and the wait before killing the process

study.title: Setup and cleanup helpers
study.locator: `tests/common.py`: `_setup_process_group` and `_cleanup_process_group` as the setup and teardown pattern behind the DDP and FSDP tests

focus: Log on every rank: rank, group, collective sequence number, tensor shape and dtype, and start and end times. Rank 0 logs alone never show the failing rank.
Sequence numbers align the same collective across ranks. A gap or a lone high number on one rank points at the call that diverged.
Timeouts bound every wait: 30 minutes default for gloo and other backends, 10 minutes for NCCL. `dist.monitored_barrier` with a short fuse names the rank that never arrives.
`dist.destroy_process_group` closes the group on each rank that reaches it. Ranks killed before teardown leave orphans holding ports; the launcher reaps them only if it tracks the processes.
units.reproduce: On 2 gloo CPU processes, log 3 collectives with sequence numbers 0, 1 and 2 plus shapes and durations on both ranks. Then delay rank 1 before a `monitored_barrier` with a 30-second timeout and show the report naming rank 1.
traps: Logging only on rank 0. The guilty rank is usually elsewhere, so rank-0 logs show a clean run that waited forever.
Keeping default timeouts during fault drills. A 30-minute fuse turns a 10-second diagnosis into a coffee break.
Reading NCCL_DEBUG output as a collective trace. It shows connectivity and call counts, not tensor values or sequence agreement.

selfTest.q: What are the default collective timeouts for NCCL and for gloo, and why do drills override them?
selfTest.a: 10 minutes for NCCL and 30 minutes for other backends including gloo. Drills use seconds so a hang reports quickly instead of stalling the session.

selfTest.q: Rank 0 logs sequence numbers 0, 1, 2 and rank 1 logs 0, 1, 1. What diverged?
selfTest.a: The third collective. Rank 1 repeated or never advanced past sequence 1, so its call sequence disagrees with rank 0 from number 2 on.

selfTest.q: A process is killed before `destroy_process_group`. What remains, and who cleans it?
selfTest.a: The dead rank never closes its group state, and orphan processes may keep holding ports or GPU memory. The launcher reaps tracked children; untracked or remote orphans need explicit cleanup.

selfTest.q: `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` shows one rank on `NET/Socket` while others use `NET/IB`. Is that a collective bug?
selfTest.a: No, it is a fabric mismatch: that rank fell back to sockets while others use InfiniBand. Fix interfaces or placement before suspecting call order.

units.title: A CPU multiprocess collective correctness suite
outcomes: Build a multiprocess suite that checks broadcast, all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter and all-to-all against single-process oracles.
Cover ranks, subgroups, dtypes and edge cases with deterministic seeds and distinct ports.
Prove that one injected fault fails loudly instead of passing silently.
units.why: Every later parallel strategy rests on these five collectives. A suite that checks them on CPU catches ordering and ownership bugs before they hide inside a trainer.

next.note: Reuse the oracle pattern for update equivalence.
Extend the suite discipline to composed plans.

study.locator: Distributed Training: `average_gradients` compared against single-process math, which is the oracle shape to copy for every collective

study.title: Equivalence test pattern
study.locator: `tests/test_ddp.py` with `tests/common.py`: the broadcast check plus the multi-step equivalence against a single-process reference

study.title: Oracle semantics for four collectives
study.locator: The problem statement: rank-ordered concatenation for `all_gather`, elementwise sums for `all_reduce`, equal contiguous chunks for `reduce_scatter`, and source-ordered blocks for `all_to_all`
study.depth: Use the statement as the oracle contract. Solve the problem itself in the earlier units.

focus: The oracle is a single-process computation: the same sums, concatenations and chunks with no communication. Every rank result must equal its oracle slice exactly.
Cover the world group plus one subgroup, two dtypes, empty and uneven inputs, and at least world sizes 2 and 4. Bugs that pass at world 2 often fail at world 4.
Fix seeds, set a short timeout, and give each concurrent run a distinct master port. Shared ports let two suites join each other.
The suite checks semantics only. Timing numbers from gloo runs must not appear as performance claims anywhere in the report.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write the suite skeleton for 4 gloo CPU processes: all five collectives asserted against the oracle on every rank. Run it green, then inject one fault such as a missing division by world size and show the suite failing on the exact assertion.
traps: Testing only world size 2. Ring wrap and subgroup indexing faults need 3 or more ranks to trigger.
Comparing only rank 0 results. Ownership bugs show on the ranks nobody asserts.
Sharing one master port across parallel suites. Ranks from different suites rendezvous together and every assertion becomes noise.

selfTest.q: Why must the oracle be single-process rather than another distributed run?
selfTest.a: Two distributed runs can share the same bug, such as a missing rescale, and agree with each other. The single-process math is independent of the communication code under test.

selfTest.q: What does a subgroup test add beyond world-group tests?
selfTest.a: It checks group construction and per-group ordering: ranks must build identical membership and issue the subgroup sequence separately from the world sequence.

selfTest.q: Which edge inputs belong in the suite, and why?
selfTest.a: Empty tensors, uneven chunk sizes, both dtypes in use, and world sizes 2 and 4. They trigger divisibility, padding and indexing paths that even splits never touch.

selfTest.q: Two suites run at once with the same port and both fail strangely. What happened?
selfTest.a: Cross-joined rendezvous: ranks from different suites formed one group. Distinct ports per run keep suites apart.

units.title: Hierarchical collectives and compressed communication with accuracy controls
outcomes: Derive the three-phase hierarchical all-reduce bytes and state when hierarchy wins.
Explain quantization, sparsification and error feedback with their accuracy controls.
State the warmup and measurement contract that makes a compression claim trustworthy.
units.why: Flat collectives waste the fast tier, and raw compression wastes accuracy. Hierarchy and accuracy-controlled compression are the two levers that survive at cluster scale.

study.title: Hierarchical all-reduce with the worked saving
study.locator: Hierarchical Communication with Hierarchical AllReduce: the three phases plus the flat 40 ms versus hierarchical 8.3 ms worked comparison

study.title: Compression, error feedback and when to use it
study.locator: Gradient Compression Under Bandwidth Scarcity with Quantization, Sparsification, Error feedback and When to use compression, including the telescoping-sum argument

study.title: Cross-node collectives and the node-bound quiz
study.locator: How Do Collectives Work on GPUs, Cross-node collectives: the fat-tree time set by node egress bandwidth, with hierarchical all-to-all

focus: Hierarchy works in three phases: reduce inside each node over the fast tier, exchange only shards between nodes over the slow tier, then redistribute inside nodes. The saving equals the bytes kept off the slow tier.
Compression only helps bandwidth-bound traffic above the crossover size. Below it the latency term is unchanged, so small routed messages gain nothing from fewer bytes.
Error feedback carries the compression residual forward, so the telescoping sum preserves the true total across steps. Naive top-k without it is biased and drifts.
One-bit and sparse schemes need a warmup in full precision plus a measured accuracy check. A byte saving without a convergence comparison is not a result.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, recompute the book flat-versus-hierarchical comparison (40 ms against 8.3 ms) from the tier bandwidths, then write the 3-step telescoping sum that shows error feedback preserving the total of the true gradients.
traps: Quoting the book H100-cluster reference values as targets. They are the authors' cluster numbers; your fabric needs its own \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and measurement.
Compressing latency-bound traffic. Shrinking a 4 KB routing message changes almost nothing because startup dominates its cost.
Skipping warmup for 1-bit schemes. Early-step statistics are unstable, so full-precision warmup plus a loss comparison is part of the method, not optional.

selfTest.q: What are the three hierarchical phases, and which bytes avoid the slow tier?
selfTest.a: Intra-node reduce, inter-node shard exchange, intra-node redistribute. Only the reduced shards cross the slow tier; the full payload never leaves the fast tier.

selfTest.q: Why does error feedback preserve the true gradient sum across steps?
selfTest.a: Each step sends the compressed value but adds the residual back into the next step input. The residuals telescope, so the cumulative sent total equals the cumulative true total plus only the final residual.

selfTest.q: A 140 GB gradient compresses to 1.4 GB. Does the operation become latency-bound?
selfTest.a: No. At 1.4 GB it still sits far above any realistic crossover size, so it stays bandwidth-bound with a proportionally smaller term.

selfTest.q: What must a compression experiment report besides the byte saving?
selfTest.a: Warmup policy, the accuracy or loss comparison against the uncompressed run, and the fabric and message regime, so the saving is tied to preserved model quality.
